newsitem.title: UK: Planned N.ireland march draws protest.
newsitem.headline: Planned N.ireland march draws protest.

text.p: Roman Catholics angry at the route of a weekend Protestant parade said on Thursday they planned a counter-march, reviving memories of sectarian tension fired by Northern Ireland parades in July.

The Bogside Residents Association grouping Catholic Irish nationalists said in a statement that the planned Apprentice Boys parade around the walls of Londonderry was a confrontation and called for a counter parade at the same location.

Spokesman Donncha MacNiallais said 13 residents of the Catholic Bogside area of Londonderry would walk along the walls at exactly the same time as 200 members of the Apprentice Boys, but denied they would try to block the parade.
"I don't think you could say that 13 people protesting could be described as an attempt to block the parade," he said.
William Moore, General Secretary of the Apprentice Boys, said: "If there is going to be a counter demonstration then it is obvious that the Bogside Residents Group is looking for confrontation.

"We hope that common sense will prevail and the people of Bogside and the nationalist people of Londonderry realise that Protestants have the right to commemorate our history and culture free from confrontation and trouble."

MacNiallaise said the "arrogant" refusal of the Apprentice Boys to negotiate over the parade was "triumphalism, coat-trailing and confrontational. Our community expects equality and parity of esteem. We are determined to ensure that these rights are accorded to us".
The organisation called on residents to give "calm and dignified support to the peaceful protest" by gathering at a nearby street when it takes place.
Saturday's march has awakened fears of fresh sectarian tension in an atmosphere charged by an Irish Republican Army (IRA) bomb attack on Britain's army headquarters in the province last week.
Police have not yet decided whether to grant permission to the Apprentice Boys to hold the parade.

The Londonderry parade was postponed in July when violence swept the province over the holding of a similar march by the Orange Order through the mainly Catholic area of the southern town of Portadown.
Protestant protests forced police to reverse a ban on the march, which went ahead, sparking a wave of Catholic protest which led to the banning of the Londonderry march.
The Apprentice Boys take their name from 13 trainee workers who slammed shut the gates of the city in the 17th century to prevent King James 11, a Catholic monarch, taking the city.
It is one of several Protestant-based organisations which annually celebrate their roots in Northern Ireland by holding marches seen by Catholics as intimidation.
